findings: The repository is a pilot backend-service scaffold using Java 25, Quarkus, Gradle Kotlin DSL, strict Clean Architecture, PostgreSQL, and rootless Podman Quadlet deployment governance.

Existing assets include Gradle and Quarkus scaffolding, container Dockerfiles, CI configuration, and a detailed DBML. No application Java sources, tests, Flyway migrations, API contracts, LikeC4 models, ADRs, or deployment directory were found.

The DBML defines a tenant-scoped Party Registry bounded context covering parties, natural-person and legal-entity details, nationalities, official identifiers, identifier schemes, and transactional outbox events. It explicitly excludes authentication, authorization, accounts, commercial roles, addresses, contacts, tax configuration, ownership, and relationship management.

The DBML is the manifest-designated persistence source of truth, but no recorded human approval or database-contract validation exists. Its presence does not authorize persistence implementation or migrations.

No authoritative product requirements, stakeholder definitions, use-case inventory, business acceptance criteria, public API contract, integration-event contract, compatibility policy, service-level objectives, retention policy, privacy classification, or operational support model were found.

Security requirements remain unresolved for authentication, authorization, trusted tenant context, encryption and HMAC key ownership and rotation, sensitive-data access, auditing, privacy, and retention.
Required strict Clean Architecture artifacts are absent, including LikeC4 context, container, and deployment views, ADRs, bounded-context ownership documentation, and explicit ports.

The build currently declares only Quarkus Arc and Quarkus test support. REST, persistence, migration, security, messaging, observability, and health capabilities have not been selected or implemented.
The CI workflow conflicts with the deployment profile by using SSH and SCP directly against the VPS instead of approved restricted deployment interfaces.
The CI workflow contains cross-service references to geographic-reference-service files and staging paths, while the referenced deploy directory and files do not exist.
The workflow publishes mutable tags without capturing an immutable OCI digest and does not demonstrate promotion of the same digest through development, staging, and production.
Required deployment readiness, liveness, smoke, stabilization, and approval-governed rollback evidence is absent.

The identified high-risk deployment and security gaps do not prevent read-only requirements specification, but they must not be treated as approved behavior or carried into implementation without resolution.
requiredActions: Elicit authoritative stakeholders, desired outcomes, use cases, business rules, functional boundaries, exclusions, and testable product acceptance criteria during specification.
Define authentication, authorization, tenant-context enforcement, encryption and HMAC key management, sensitive-data handling, auditing, privacy, and retention requirements.
Define public API and integration-event boundaries, including Geographic Reference Service interactions and outbox consumer expectations.
Define measurable performance, availability, resilience, observability, recovery, health, and operational support requirements.
Keep persistence implementation and Flyway migration work blocked until explicit DBML confirmation and database-contract validation are recorded.
Have the designated architecture agent produce the required LikeC4 views, ADRs, bounded-context ownership, execution-model decision, and explicit ports after requirements are established.
Before deployment work, remove cross-service references, supply party-registry-service deployment assets, and replace direct SSH/SCP behavior with the approved restricted deployment mechanism.
Before release promotion, implement immutable OCI digest capture and same-digest promotion with required health, readiness, smoke, stabilization, and rollback controls.
Add applicable unit, integration, architecture, API-contract, security, and performance validation in their designated downstream phases.
